title: All the Defilements
html:
• Majjhima Nikāya 2 Middle Discourses 2

Sabbāsavasutta All the Defilements Every Vice

Evaṁ me sutaṁ—So I have heard. Thus have I heard. ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. At one time the Buddha was living at Sāvatthi, in Jeta’s grove, at Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants, There the Buddha addressed the monks: “bhikkhavo”ti. “Mendicants!” “Monks!”

“Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṁ. “Venerable sir,” they replied. “Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha. Bhagavā etadavoca: The Buddha said this: The Buddha said this:

“sabbāsavasaṁvarapariyāyaṁ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi. “Mendicants, I will teach you the explanation of the restraint of all defilements. “Monks, I will teach you how to control every vice. Taṁ suṇātha, sādhukaṁ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. Listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.” Listen to this and carefully apply your mind to it; I will speak.”

“Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṁ. “Yes, sir,” they replied. “Yes, Bhante,” those monks replied to the Buddha. Bhagavā etadavoca: The Buddha said this: The Buddha said this:

“Jānato ahaṁ, bhikkhave, passato āsavānaṁ khayaṁ vadāmi, no ajānato no apassato. “Mendicants, I say that the ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see. “Monks, I say that the elimination of vices is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. Kiñca, bhikkhave, jānato kiñca passato āsavānaṁ khayaṁ vadāmi? For one who knows and sees what? For one who knows and sees what? Yoniso ca manasikāraṁ ayoniso ca manasikāraṁ. Rational application of mind and irrational application of mind. Application of mind based on an understanding of causality, and application of mind not based on an understanding of causality. Ayoniso, bhikkhave, manasikaroto anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjanti, uppannā ca āsavā pavaḍḍhanti; When you apply the mind irrationally, defilements arise, and once arisen they grow. Monks, when one applies one’s mind without an understanding of causality, one develops new vices, and one’s old vices grow stronger. yoniso ca kho, bhikkhave, manasikaroto anuppannā ceva āsavā na uppajjanti, uppannā ca āsavā pahīyanti. When you apply the mind rationally, defilements don’t arise, and those that have already arisen are given up. Monks, when one applies one’s mind based on an understanding of causality, one does not develop new vices, and one’s old vices are abandoned.

Atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā saṁvarā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā paṭisevanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā adhivāsanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā parivajjanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā vinodanā pahātabbā, atthi āsavā bhāvanā pahātabbā. Some defilements should be given up by seeing, some by restraint, some by using, some by enduring, some by avoiding, some by dispelling, and some by developing. Monks, there are vices to be abandoned by seeing, vices to be abandoned by self-control, vices to be abandoned by using, vices to be abandoned by enduring, vices to be abandoned by avoiding, vices to be abandoned by removing, and vices to be abandoned by cultivating.

1. Dassanāpahātabbaāsava 1. Defilements Given Up by Seeing Vices to be Abandoned by Seeing

Katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbā? And what are the defilements that should be given up by seeing? Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by seeing? Idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṁ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido ariyadhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṁ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinīto—Take an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve not seen true persons, and are neither skilled nor trained in the teaching of the true persons. In this case, monks, an uneducated commoner—one who does not see noble people and is not skilled and disciplined in the teachings of noble people, and who does not see good people and is not skilled and disciplined in the teachings of good people— manasikaraṇīye dhamme nappajānāti, amanasikaraṇīye dhamme nappajānāti. They don’t understand to which things they should apply the mind and to which things they should not apply the mind. does not understand what the mind should not be applied to and what the mind should be applied to. So manasikaraṇīye dhamme appajānanto amanasikaraṇīye dhamme appajānanto, ye dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā, te dhamme manasi karoti, ye dhammā manasikaraṇīyā te dhamme na manasi karoti. So they apply the mind to things they shouldn’t and don’t apply the mind to things they should. Since they do not understand what the mind should be applied and what the mind should not be applied to, they apply their mind to what they should not apply it to and they do not apply their mind to what they should apply it to.

Katame ca, bhikkhave, dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme manasi karoti? And what are the things to which they apply the mind but should not? And, monks, what should the mind not be applied to that they apply their mind to? Yassa, bhikkhave, dhamme manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā kāmāsavo pavaḍḍhati; They are the things that, when the mind is applied to them, give rise to unarisen defilements and make arisen defilements grow: the defilements of sensual desire, Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, causes a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to grow stronger; anuppanno vā bhavāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā bhavāsavo pavaḍḍhati; desire to be reborn, or causes a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to grow stronger; anuppanno vā avijjāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā avijjāsavo pavaḍḍhati—and ignorance. or causes a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to grow stronger; ime dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme manasi karoti. These are the things to which they apply the mind but should not. this is what the mind should not be applied to that they apply their mind to.

Katame ca, bhikkhave, dhammā manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme na manasi karoti? And what are the things to which they do not apply the mind but should? And, monks, what should the mind be applied to that they do not apply their mind to? Yassa, bhikkhave, dhamme manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā kāmāsavo pahīyati; They are the things that, when the mind is applied to them, do not give rise to unarisen defilements and give up arisen defilements: the defilements of sensual desire, Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, does not cause a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to be abandoned; anuppanno vā bhavāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā bhavāsavo pahīyati; desire to be reborn, or does not cause a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to be abandoned; anuppanno vā avijjāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā avijjāsavo pahīyati—and ignorance. or does not cause a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to be abandoned; ime dhammā manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme na manasi karoti. These are the things to which they do not apply the mind but should. this is what the mind should be applied to that they do not apply their mind to.

Tassa amanasikaraṇīyānaṁ dhammānaṁ manasikārā manasikaraṇīyānaṁ dhammānaṁ amanasikārā anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjanti uppannā ca āsavā pavaḍḍhanti. Because of applying the mind to what they should not and not applying the mind to what they should, unarisen defilements arise and arisen defilements grow. So when they apply their mind to that which it should not be applied to and do not apply their mind to that which it should be applied to, they develop new vices and their old vices grow stronger.

So evaṁ ayoniso manasi karoti: This is how they apply the mind irrationally: This is how they apply their mind without an understanding of causality: ‘ahosiṁ nu kho ahaṁ atītamaddhānaṁ? Na nu kho ahosiṁ atītamaddhānaṁ? Kiṁ nu kho ahosiṁ atītamaddhānaṁ? Kathaṁ nu kho ahosiṁ atītamaddhānaṁ? Kiṁ hutvā kiṁ ahosiṁ nu kho ahaṁ atītamaddhānaṁ? ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? After being what, what did I become in the past? they think, ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having done what, what did I become in the past?’ Bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṁ anāgatamaddhānaṁ? Na nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṁ? Kiṁ nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṁ? Kathaṁ nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṁ? Kiṁ hutvā kiṁ bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṁ anāgatamaddhānan’ti? Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? After being what, what will I become in the future?’ ‘Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having done what, what will I become in the future?’ Etarahi vā paccuppannamaddhānaṁ ajjhattaṁ kathaṅkathī hoti: Or they are undecided about the present thus: Or they are confused about the present: ‘ahaṁ nu khosmi? No nu khosmi? Kiṁ nu khosmi? Kathaṁ nu khosmi? Ayaṁ nu kho satto kuto āgato? So kuhiṁ gāmī bhavissatī’ti? ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? This sentient being—where did it come from? And where will it go?’ ‘Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? Where did this being come from? Where will it go from here?’

Tassa evaṁ ayoniso manasikaroto channaṁ diṭṭhīnaṁ aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjati. When they apply the mind irrationally in this way, one of the following six views arises in them and is taken as a genuine fact. When one applies one’s mind in this way, one of six beliefs arises: ‘Atthi me attā’ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; The view: ‘My self survives.’ The belief ‘I have a soul’ arises and seems true and certain. ‘natthi me attā’ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; The view: ‘My self does not survive.’ Or the belief ‘I do not have a soul’ arises and seems true and certain. ‘attanāva attānaṁ sañjānāmī’ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; The view: ‘I perceive the self with the self.’ Or the belief ‘Using the soul, I perceive the soul’ arises and seems true and certain. ‘attanāva anattānaṁ sañjānāmī’ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; The view: ‘I perceive what is not-self with the self.’ Or the belief ‘Using the soul, I perceive what is not the soul’ arises and seems true and certain. ‘anattanāva attānaṁ sañjānāmī’ti vā assa saccato thetato diṭṭhi uppajjati; The view: ‘I perceive the self with what is not-self.’ Or the belief ‘Using what is not the soul, I perceive the soul’ arises and seems true and certain. atha vā panassa evaṁ diṭṭhi hoti: Or they have such a view: Or they have this belief: ‘yo me ayaṁ attā vado vedeyyo tatra tatra kalyāṇapāpakānaṁ kammānaṁ vipākaṁ paṭisaṁvedeti so kho pana me ayaṁ attā nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo sassatisamaṁ tatheva ṭhassatī’ti. ‘This self of mine is he, the one who speaks, the one who knows, who experiences the results of good and bad deeds in all the different realms. This self is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable, and will last forever and ever.’ ‘This is my soul; it speaks, it feels, it experiences the results of good and evil actions; and this soul of mine is permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and will remain like this for eternity.’ Idaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, diṭṭhigataṁ diṭṭhigahanaṁ diṭṭhikantāraṁ diṭṭhivisūkaṁ diṭṭhivipphanditaṁ diṭṭhisaṁyojanaṁ. This is called a misconception, the thicket of views, the desert of views, the twist of views, the dodge of views, the fetter of views. Monks, this is called settling on a belief, becoming entangled in a belief, becoming disturbed by a belief, becoming agitated by a belief, becoming shackled by a belief. Diṭṭhisaṁyojanasaṁyutto, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano na parimuccati jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi; An unlearned ordinary person who is fettered by views is not freed from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. Shackled by a belief, monks, the uneducated commoner is not freed from birth, decrepitude, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and anguish; ‘na parimuccati dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi. They’re not freed from suffering, I say. they are not freed from suffering, I say.

Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako—Monks, an educated disciple of the noble ones— ariyānaṁ dassāvī ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto, sappurisānaṁ dassāvī sappurisadhammassa kovido sappurisadhamme suvinīto—But take a learned noble disciple who has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and trained in the teaching of the noble ones. They’ve seen true persons, and are skilled and trained in the teaching of the true persons. one who sees noble people and is skilled and disciplined in the teachings of noble people, and who sees good people and is skilled and disciplined in the teachings of good people— manasikaraṇīye dhamme pajānāti amanasikaraṇīye dhamme pajānāti. They understand to which things they should apply the mind and to which things they should not apply the mind. understands what the mind the should be applied to and what the mind should not be applied to. So manasikaraṇīye dhamme pajānanto amanasikaraṇīye dhamme pajānanto ye dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā te dhamme na manasi karoti, ye dhammā manasikaraṇīyā te dhamme manasi karoti. So they apply the mind to things they should and don’t apply the mind to things they shouldn’t. Since they understand what the mind should be applied and what the mind should not be applied to, they do not apply their mind to what they should not apply it to and they do apply their mind to what they should apply it to.

Katame ca, bhikkhave, dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme na manasi karoti? And what are the things to which they don’t apply the mind and should not? And, monks, what should the mind not be applied to that they do not apply their mind to? Yassa, bhikkhave, dhamme manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā kāmāsavo pavaḍḍhati; They are the things that, when the mind is applied to them, give rise to unarisen defilements and make arisen defilements grow: the defilements of sensual desire, Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, causes a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to grow stronger; anuppanno vā bhavāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā bhavāsavo pavaḍḍhati; desire to be reborn, or causes a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to grow stronger; anuppanno vā avijjāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā avijjāsavo pavaḍḍhati—and ignorance. or causes a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to grow stronger; ime dhammā na manasikaraṇīyā, ye dhamme na manasi karoti. These are the things to which they don’t apply the mind and should not. this is what the mind should not be applied to that they do not apply their mind to.

Katame ca, bhikkhave, dhammā manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme manasi karoti? And what are the things to which they do apply the mind and should? And, monks, what should the mind be applied to that they apply their mind to? Yassa, bhikkhave, dhamme manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā kāmāsavo pahīyati; They are the things that, when the mind is applied to them, do not give rise to unarisen defilements and give up arisen defilements: the defilements of sensual desire, Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, does not cause a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to be abandoned; anuppanno vā bhavāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā bhavāsavo pahīyati; desire to be reborn, or does not cause a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to be abandoned; anuppanno vā avijjāsavo na uppajjati, uppanno vā avijjāsavo pahīyati—and ignorance. or does not cause a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to be abandoned; ime dhammā manasikaraṇīyā ye dhamme manasi karoti. These are the things to which they do apply the mind and should. this is what the mind should be applied to that they apply their mind to.

Tassa amanasikaraṇīyānaṁ dhammānaṁ amanasikārā manasikaraṇīyānaṁ dhammānaṁ manasikārā anuppannā ceva āsavā na uppajjanti, uppannā ca āsavā pahīyanti. Because of not applying the mind to what they should not and applying the mind to what they should, unarisen defilements don’t arise and arisen defilements are given up. So when they do not apply their mind to that which it should not be applied to and do apply their mind to that which it should be applied to, they do not develop new vices and their old vices are abandoned.

So ‘idaṁ dukkhan’ti yoniso manasi karoti, ‘ayaṁ dukkhasamudayo’ti yoniso manasi karoti, ‘ayaṁ dukkhanirodho’ti yoniso manasi karoti, ‘ayaṁ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yoniso manasi karoti. They rationally apply the mind: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’. They apply their mind based on an understanding of causality in this way: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the cause suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the path of practice which leads to the cessation of suffering.’ Tassa evaṁ yoniso manasikaroto tīṇi saṁyojanāni pahīyanti—And as they do so, they give up three fetters: Applying the mind based on an understanding of causality in this way, three shackles are abandoned: sakkāyadiṭṭhi, vicikicchā, sīlabbataparāmāso. substantialist view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances. belief in self-existence, skepticism, and misapprehension of habitual practices. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbā. These are called the defilements that should be given up by seeing. Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by seeing.

2. Saṁvarāpahātabbaāsava 2. Defilements Given Up by Restraint Vices to be Abandoned by Self-Control

Katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā saṁvarā pahātabbā? And what are the defilements that should be given up by restraint? Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by self-control? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cakkhundriyasaṁvarasaṁvuto viharati. Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, lives restraining the eye faculty. In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk practices self-control regarding the sense of sight. Yañhissa, bhikkhave, cakkhundriyasaṁvaraṁ asaṁvutassa viharato uppajjeyyuṁ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, cakkhundriyasaṁvaraṁ saṁvutassa viharato evaṁsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without restraint of the eye faculty do not arise when there is such restraint. Because, monks, when one does not practice self-control regarding the sense of sight, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices self-control regarding the sense of sight, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present. Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso sotindriyasaṁvarasaṁvuto viharati …pe… Reflecting rationally, they live restraining the ear faculty … Contemplating causality, a monk practices self-control regarding the sense of sound… ghānindriyasaṁvarasaṁvuto viharati …pe… the nose faculty … sense of smell… jivhindriyasaṁvarasaṁvuto viharati …pe… the tongue faculty … sense of taste… kāyindriyasaṁvarasaṁvuto viharati …pe… the body faculty … sense of touch… manindriyasaṁvarasaṁvuto viharati. the mind faculty. sense of cognition. Yañhissa, bhikkhave, manindriyasaṁvaraṁ asaṁvutassa viharato uppajjeyyuṁ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, manindriyasaṁvaraṁ saṁvutassa viharato evaṁsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without restraint of the mind faculty do not arise when there is such restraint. Because, monks, when one does not practice self-control regarding the sense of cognition, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices self-control regarding the sense of cognition, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.

Yañhissa, bhikkhave, saṁvaraṁ asaṁvutassa viharato uppajjeyyuṁ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, saṁvaraṁ saṁvutassa viharato evaṁsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without restraint do not arise when there is such restraint. Because, monks, when one does not practice self-control, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices self-control, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā saṁvarā pahātabbā. These are called the defilements that should be given up by restraint. Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by self-control.

3. Paṭisevanāpahātabbaāsava 3. Defilements Given Up by Using Vices to be Abandoned by Using

Katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā paṭisevanā pahātabbā? And what are the defilements that should be given up by using? Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by using? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṁ paṭisevati: Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, makes use of robes: In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk uses their robe ‘yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāya, uṇhassa paṭighātāya, ḍaṁsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassānaṁ paṭighātāya, yāvadeva hirikopīnappaṭicchādanatthaṁ’. ‘Only for the sake of warding off cold and heat; for warding off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; and for covering up the private parts.’ just for the purpose of not getting too cold; not getting too hot; not coming in contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and reptiles; and to cover the genitals.

Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso piṇḍapātaṁ paṭisevati: Reflecting rationally, they make use of almsfood: Contemplating causality, a monk uses almsfood ‘neva davāya, na madāya, na maṇḍanāya, na vibhūsanāya, yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāya, vihiṁsūparatiyā, brahmacariyānuggahāya, iti purāṇañca vedanaṁ paṭihaṅkhāmi navañca vedanaṁ na uppādessāmi, yātrā ca me bhavissati anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro ca’. ‘Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’ not for entertainment, not for intoxication, not for beauty, not for decoration; but just for the sustenance and health of their body, and to support the spiritual life; thinking, ‘In this way, I will remove old feelings and I will not produce new feelings, so that I will be blameless and comfortable.’

Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso senāsanaṁ paṭisevati: Reflecting rationally, they make use of lodgings: Contemplating causality, a monk uses their dwelling ‘yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāya, uṇhassa paṭighātāya, ḍaṁsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassānaṁ paṭighātāya, yāvadeva utuparissayavinodanapaṭisallānārāmatthaṁ’. ‘Only for the sake of warding off cold and heat; for warding off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; to shelter from harsh weather and to enjoy retreat.’ just for the purpose of not getting too cold; not getting too hot; not coming in contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and reptiles; protection from weather; and to enjoy personal retreat.

Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṁ paṭisevati: Reflecting rationally, they make use of medicines and supplies for the sick: Contemplating causality, a monk uses medicines and medicinal supplies ‘yāvadeva uppannānaṁ veyyābādhikānaṁ vedanānaṁ paṭighātāya, abyābajjhaparamatāya’. ‘Only for the sake of warding off the pains of illness and to promote good health.’ just for the purpose of preventing affliction and to be free from illness.

Yañhissa, bhikkhave, appaṭisevato uppajjeyyuṁ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, paṭisevato evaṁsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without using these things do not arise when they are used. Because, monks, when one does not practice proper use, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices proper use, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā paṭisevanā pahātabbā. These are called the defilements that should be given up by using. Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by using.

4. Adhivāsanāpahātabbaāsava 4. Defilements Given Up by Enduring Vices to be Abandoned by Enduring

Katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā adhivāsanā pahātabbā? And what are the defilements that should be given up by enduring? Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by enduring? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso khamo hoti sītassa uṇhassa, jighacchāya pipāsāya. Ḍaṁsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassānaṁ, duruttānaṁ durāgatānaṁ vacanapathānaṁ, uppannānaṁ sārīrikānaṁ vedanānaṁ dukkhānaṁ tibbānaṁ kharānaṁ kaṭukānaṁ asātānaṁ amanāpānaṁ pāṇaharānaṁ adhivāsakajātiko hoti. Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, endures cold, heat, hunger, and thirst. They endure the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles. They endure rude and unwelcome criticism. And they put up with physical pain—sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening. In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk endures cold and heat; hunger and thirst; contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and reptiles; improper and unwelcome statements; physical sensations that are painful, sharp, harsh, severe, uncomfortable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.

Yañhissa, bhikkhave, anadhivāsayato uppajjeyyuṁ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, adhivāsayato evaṁsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without enduring these things do not arise when they are endured. Because, monks, when one does not endure, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one endures, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā adhivāsanā pahātabbā. These are called the defilements that should be given up by enduring. Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by enduring.

5. Parivajjanāpahātabbaāsava 5. Defilements Given Up by Avoiding Vices to be Abandoned by Avoiding

Katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā parivajjanā pahātabbā? And what are the defilements that should be given up by avoiding? Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by avoiding? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso caṇḍaṁ hatthiṁ parivajjeti, caṇḍaṁ assaṁ parivajjeti, caṇḍaṁ goṇaṁ parivajjeti, caṇḍaṁ kukkuraṁ parivajjeti, ahiṁ khāṇuṁ kaṇṭakaṭṭhānaṁ sobbhaṁ papātaṁ candanikaṁ oḷigallaṁ. Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, avoids a wild elephant, a wild horse, a wild ox, a wild dog, a snake, a stump, thorny ground, a pit, a cliff, a swamp, and a sewer. In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk avoids a wild elephant, a wild horse, a wild ox, a wild dog, a snake, a stump, a thorn-bush, a pit, a precipice, a swamp, a sewer; Yathārūpe anāsane nisinnaṁ yathārūpe agocare carantaṁ yathārūpe pāpake mitte bhajantaṁ viññū sabrahmacārī pāpakesu ṭhānesu okappeyyuṁ, so tañca anāsanaṁ tañca agocaraṁ te ca pāpake mitte paṭisaṅkhā yoniso parivajjeti. Reflecting rationally, they avoid sitting on inappropriate seats, walking in inappropriate neighborhoods, and mixing with bad friends—whatever sensible spiritual companions would believe to be a bad setting. contemplating causality, a monk avoids sitting in improper places, going to improper places, or associating with evil friends, since such behavior might give one’s discerning spiritual companions cause for suspicion.

Yañhissa, bhikkhave, aparivajjayato uppajjeyyuṁ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, parivajjayato evaṁsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without avoiding these things do not arise when they are avoided. Because, monks, when one does not avoid such things, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one avoids such things, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā parivajjanā pahātabbā. These are called the defilements that should be given up by avoiding. Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by avoiding.

6. Vinodanāpahātabbaāsava 6. Defilements Given Up by Dispelling Vices to be Abandoned by Removing

Katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā vinodanā pahātabbā? And what are the defilements that should be given up by dispelling? Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by removing? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso uppannaṁ kāmavitakkaṁ nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti byantīkaroti anabhāvaṁ gameti, uppannaṁ byāpādavitakkaṁ …pe… uppannaṁ vihiṁsāvitakkaṁ …pe… uppannuppanne pāpake akusale dhamme nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti byantīkaroti anabhāvaṁ gameti. Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, doesn’t tolerate a sensual, malicious, or cruel thought that has arisen, but gives it up, dispels it, eliminates it, and obliterates it. They don’t tolerate any bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen, but give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them. In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk does not tolerate a sensual thought that is present, but instead abandons it, removes it, terminates it, and annihilates it; does not tolerate an aversive thought that is present, but instead abandons it, removes it, terminates it, and annihilates it; does not tolerate a malicious thought that is present, but instead abandons it, removes it, terminates it, and annihilates it; does not tolerate any harmful, unwholesome qualities that are present, but instead abandons them, removes them, terminates them, and annihilates them.

Yañhissa, bhikkhave, avinodayato uppajjeyyuṁ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, vinodayato evaṁsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without dispelling these things do not arise when they are dispelled. Because, monks, when one does not remove such things, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one removes such things, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā vinodanā pahātabbā. These are called the defilements that should be given up by dispelling. Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by removing.

7. Bhāvanāpahātabbaāsava 7. Defilements Given Up by Developing Vices to be Abandoned by Cultivating

Katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā bhāvanā pahātabbā? And what are the defilements that should be given up by developing? Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by cultivating? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso satisambojjhaṅgaṁ bhāveti vivekanissitaṁ virāganissitaṁ nirodhanissitaṁ vossaggapariṇāmiṁ; Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, develops the awakening factors of mindfulness, In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk cultivates the mindfulness factor of awakening, which is dependent on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and culminates in relinquishment; paṭisaṅkhā yoniso dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṁ bhāveti …pe… investigation of principles, contemplating causality, a monk cultivates the investigation factor of awakening… vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṁ bhāveti … energy, the determination factor of awakening… pītisambojjhaṅgaṁ bhāveti … rapture, the euphoria factor of awakening… passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṁ bhāveti … tranquility, the tranquility factor of awakening… samādhisambojjhaṅgaṁ bhāveti … immersion, the concentration factor of awakening… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṁ bhāveti vivekanissitaṁ virāganissitaṁ nirodhanissitaṁ vossaggapariṇāmiṁ. and equanimity, which rely on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripen as letting go. the equanimity factor of awakening, which is dependent on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and culminates in relinquishment;

Yañhissa, bhikkhave, abhāvayato uppajjeyyuṁ āsavā vighātapariḷāhā, bhāvayato evaṁsa te āsavā vighātapariḷāhā na honti. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in someone who lives without developing these things do not arise when they are developed. Because, monks, when one does not cultivate such things, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one cultivates such things, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā bhāvanā pahātabbā. These are called the defilements that should be given up by developing. Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by cultivating.

Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno ye āsavā dassanā pahātabbā te dassanā pahīnā honti, ye āsavā saṁvarā pahātabbā te saṁvarā pahīnā honti, ye āsavā paṭisevanā pahātabbā te paṭisevanā pahīnā honti, ye āsavā adhivāsanā pahātabbā te adhivāsanā pahīnā honti, ye āsavā parivajjanā pahātabbā te parivajjanā pahīnā honti, ye āsavā vinodanā pahātabbā te vinodanā pahīnā honti, ye āsavā bhāvanā pahātabbā te bhāvanā pahīnā honti; Now, take a mendicant who, by seeing, has given up the defilements that should be given up by seeing. By restraint, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by restraint. By using, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by using. By enduring, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by enduring. By avoiding, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by avoiding. By dispelling, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by dispelling. By developing, they’ve given up the defilements that should be given up by developing. Monks, when a monk has abandoned by seeing the vices to be abandoned by seeing, has abandoned by self-control the vices to be abandoned by self-control, has abandoned by using the vices to be abandoned by using, has abandoned by enduring the vices to be abandoned by enduring, has abandoned by avoiding the vices to be abandoned by avoiding, has abandoned by removing the vices to be abandoned by removing, and has abandoned by cultivating the vices to be abandoned by cultivating, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave: ‘bhikkhu sabbāsavasaṁvarasaṁvuto viharati, acchecchi taṇhaṁ, vivattayi saṁyojanaṁ, sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā’”ti. They’re called a mendicant who lives having restrained all defilements, who has cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.” that monk is called a monk who has controlled every vice, cut off craving, opened the shackles, and through a correct comprehension of conceit has put an end to suffering.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. That is what the Buddha said. This is what the Buddha said. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṁ abhinandunti. Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said. Satisfied, those monks rejoiced in the Buddha’s statement.

Sabbāsavasuttaṁ niṭṭhitaṁ dutiyaṁ.
